title: Rational Expressions
summary: A rational expression is a fraction of polynomials. Simplify by factoring and cancelling; multiply/divide as with fractions; add/subtract over a common denominator. Watch for excluded values that make a denominator zero.

excluded value.plain: An $x$ that makes a denominator zero.

common denominator.plain: A shared bottom to add/subtract fractions.
common denominator.in_class: Least common multiple of the denominators.

complex fraction.in_class: Clear by multiplying by the LCD of the inner fractions.

least common denominator.in_class: Built from each distinct factor to its highest power.

reciprocal (division).plain: Divide by multiplying by the flip.

cancel factors.plain: Remove a factor common to top and bottom.

concept_sections.heading: Simplifying
concept_sections.explanation: Factor numerator and denominator, then cancel factors they share. Note the excluded values before you cancel — they stay excluded.
math_steps: State excluded values (where the original bottom was 0).

concept_sections.heading: Multiplying and dividing
concept_sections.explanation: Multiply straight across (factor and cancel first to keep it small). Divide by multiplying by the reciprocal.
math_steps: For division, flip the second fraction first.

concept_sections.heading: Common denominators
concept_sections.explanation: To add or subtract, build the least common denominator from each distinct factor at its highest power, rewrite each fraction, then combine numerators.
math_steps: Find the LCD from the factored denominators.
Rewrite each fraction over the LCD.

concept_sections.heading: Complex fractions
concept_sections.explanation: A fraction containing fractions clears by multiplying top and bottom by the LCD of the inner fractions, collapsing it to a single ratio.
math_steps: Find the LCD of the small fractions.
Multiply numerator and denominator by it.

concept_sections.heading: Excluded values and domain
concept_sections.explanation: Any $x$ making an original denominator zero is excluded, even if it cancels. Always list these restrictions with the answer.
math_steps: Set each original denominator to zero.
Keep them out of the domain of the simplified form.

real_world_examples.title: Combining work rates
real_world_examples.scenario: Two workers finish a job at different speeds.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Their combined rate adds rational expressions $\tfrac1a+\tfrac1b$ over a common denominator.

real_world_examples.title: Average speed round trip
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The average uses a rational expression that simplifies with a common denominator.

real_world_examples.title: Mixing concentrations
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The resulting concentration is a rational expression in the amounts mixed.
